messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Renée Calloway is a sixty-six-year-old widowed woman who has worked as a model for most of her adult life, a career that has demanded a precise and unforgiving awareness of her own body and presentation. She was referred for psychological assessment following a traumatic incident that occurred approximately eight months ago, when, while driving to an early-morning fitting in poor visibility conditions, she struck a cyclist who had entered the road without warning. The cyclist, a young man, sustained a fractured pelvis and a serious head injury. Renée was not cited for reckless driving, and witnesses confirmed she had been travelling within the speed limit, yet none of this has offered her any relief. She remembers the sound before she saw him — a dull, terrible impact — and the way she sat frozen in the driver's seat for what felt like minutes before she was able to move. It is that frozen moment she cannot forgive herself for. She believes, with a certainty that no amount of external reassurance has softened, that she should have reacted faster, that she should have somehow seen him sooner, that she should have done more in the immediate aftermath than stand at the roadside while others called for help.

In the months since, Renée has described a persistent state of physiological vigilance that has reshaped the texture of her daily life. Her body feels constantly braced, as though poised at the edge of the next catastrophe, and she has not been able to fully relax even in her apartment, even in moments that she recognises intellectually as safe. She wakes early and lies rigid in the dark, her muscles tight, her attention scanning. Concentration has become effortful in a way it never was before; she has missed call times, forgotten fittings, and had to ask photographers to repeat directions she would once have absorbed instantly. On set — an environment that once felt like a second home — she now finds herself hyperaware of movement in her peripheral vision, of cars passing on the street outside the studio, of any sudden shift in the room. The professional composure she has spent decades cultivating feels increasingly like a performance she can barely sustain.

What has proved most corrosive, however, is the way this constant state of alertness feeds directly into the conclusions she draws about herself. When her body will not settle, when she startles at a car horn or loses the thread of a conversation mid-sentence, Renée does not read these as symptoms of a traumatised nervous system — she reads them as evidence. The hypervigilance becomes, in her mind, proof of her fundamental inadequacy: a composed, competent person, she reasons, would not be falling apart like this. The relentless tension in her body, the failure to concentrate, the inability to simply be calm — each one confirms what she has already decided about herself. She has come to believe, with quiet but immovable conviction, that someone else — someone more capable, more alert, more deserving of the life she has been given — would never have been in that situation at all. She feels permanently humiliated, not in a social sense, but in something deeper and more private: a sense that the incident has exposed something that was always true about her and can never now be unseen.

She will never forgive herself for not doing more, she has said this in session more than once, in the same flat tone, as though reading from a verdict already handed down. She has largely stopped driving, which has complicated her work significantly, requiring her to arrange car services for early calls in ways that draw attention to a limitation she finds shameful. She has told no one in her professional circle what happened.

What finally brought Renée to seek help was a conversation with her daughter, who told her plainly that she seemed to have disappeared. What she is most afraid of, she said at the end of the first session, is that she is right about herself. What she is hoping for, though she offered this more quietly, is that she might be wrong.
